title: The du'a of Ta'if
hook: in an orchard outside Ta'if he prays: to You I complain of my weakness; if You are not angry with me, I don't mind (sirah)
carry: if you're not angry, I don't mind

segments.voice: Yesterday, stoned at Ta'if. Your line was: he walked on. After your last no, what was the next step you took? Day seven hundred fifty-one.

The crowd has fallen back. He's sitting in the shade of a vine, against the wall of an orchard that belongs to two men of Quraysh. He's been refused by three leaders, jeered at by a town, and he has nowhere obvious to go next. What would anyone say, alone, in a moment like that? A complaint about the people of Ta'if would make sense. A plea to be avenged would make sense. Ibn Ishaq records something else. Today: the du'a of Ta'if.
screen: `IN THE SHADE OF A VINE.` → `NOWHERE TO GO.` → `WHAT DOES HE SAY?`

segments.voice: A du'a is a personal prayer, words addressed to Allah in a person's own need, as opposed to the set prayer, the salah. This one, as Ibn Ishaq gives it, begins with a complaint, but not against Thaqif. He complains to Allah of his own weakness: his lack of strength, his lack of means, how small he has become in people's eyes. Then he turns. He calls Allah the most merciful of the merciful, the Lord of the weak, and asks: to whom are You leaving me? To a stranger who will scowl at me, or an enemy given power over me? And then comes today's line. If You are not angry with me, he says, I don't mind. I don't care what happens, as long as You're not displeased. Your well-being, the ease You give, is wider for me. Look at the order of that. First, honesty: I am weak, I have little, people look down on me. No pretending. Then a question, almost a child's question: who are You handing me to? And only then the turn, which isn't that the pain stops mattering, but that it's measured against one thing. If the relationship with Allah is whole, the rest can be borne. Notice what is missing, too. No curse on Ta'if. No request that the town be punished. That restraint will matter in two days. A note on the source: this du'a comes from the sirah, through Ibn Ishaq, not from Bukhari or Muslim, and hadith scholars have discussed the strength of its chain. Its words are still said today, in hard times.
screen: `A DU'A: A PRAYER IN ONE'S OWN NEED.` · `FIRST: I AM WEAK.` · `TO WHOM ARE YOU LEAVING ME?` · `NO CURSE ON TA'IF.` · then, large: `IF YOU ARE NOT ANGRY, I DON'T MIND.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray from weakness, or, if you don't pray, speak from it. Sit still. Let your hands rest open in your lap. Name, silently, three honest things: where your strength has run low, where you don't have what you need, where you feel small in other people's eyes. Don't dress them up. Then let them sit there, said. If you pray, you can bring those three things to Allah in your own words, as plainly as he did, and if you know the words of the du'a of Ta'if, you can say them. If you don't pray, just notice what it's like to say them without defending yourself. The bell holds the time.
The du'a of Ta'if. In an orchard, after rejection, he complains to Allah of his own weakness and says: if You are not angry with me, I don't mind. Today's word.
Your line: if you're not angry, I don't mind. Today, when something goes badly, ask which opinion actually matters most to you, and let that be the measure. Day seven hundred fifty-one.

howItsDone: The du'a of Ta'if is taught in sirah study alongside the journey to Ta'if, and Muslims say its words in times of hardship or rejection.

fork.setup: you're him, alone by an orchard wall after being driven out of a town. you begin to pray. what do you complain of first?
options: the cruelty of the people of Ta'if.
fork.reveal: in Ibn Ishaq's account, the complaint is of his own weakness, lack of means, and lowliness before people.

original.note: Arabic: calling on Allah; a personal prayer, distinct from the set salah.

trapdoor: what you thought: a prayer for help against enemies.
what it means: an honest complaint of weakness, ending in: if You are not angry with me, I don't mind.
what a scholar hears: a sirah report through Ibn Ishaq, not in Bukhari or Muslim, whose chain hadith scholars have discussed.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the orchard of Utba and Shayba; the du'a: complaint of weakness, 'to whom do You entrust me', 'if You are not angry with me I do not care')

notes: The du'a is paraphrased throughout; no translation is quoted (Guillaume 1955 is under copyright). Confirm the paraphrase is faithful, especially 'Your protection is wider for me'.
The script states hadith scholars 'have discussed the strength of its chain' without naming a grading; a Keeper may want to name the grading or soften further.
'Its words are still said today' is kept general on purpose under the claims rule.
The practice invites saying the du'a's own words only if the listener already knows them; no new prayer is written.
The orchard owners (Utba and Shayba, sons of Rabi'a) are referred to as 'two men of Quraysh'; they are named tomorrow.
